newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso sings praises of economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso sings praises of economic reform.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso spelled out the achievements of his inflation-busting economic plan on Monday, one day before its third anniversary.

In a television address, Cardoso also called again on lawmakers to approve reforms that have been stuck in Congress for two years. The reforms are considered vital to Cardoso's attempts to turn Brazil into an economic powerhouse.

"Brazil continues to change for the better," the president said. "Since 1994 the economy has grown by nearly 14 percent. Inflation keeps on falling. ... It is in this mood of optmism that I want to remind you that the Real Plan is three years old."

Cardoso was finance minister in 1994 when he laid the groundwork for the Real Plan, named for Brazil's new currency unit, the real. The plan's instant success in cutting rampant inflation helped him cruise to victory in presidential elections later that year.

But unlike previous economic "miracles" in Brazil, the Real Plan has not crumpled, and inflation fell to under 10 percent in 1996, its lowest level since 1957. Investors see the country as one of the world's hottest opportunities, with booming financial markets and with multibillion-dollar privatizations in the pipeline.
The plan remains popular among Brazilians. A recent poll found 74 percent supported it, making Cardoso a firm favorite to win re-election in next year's presidential race.
In his address, Cardoso reeled off a list of statistics that showed the number of people living in poverty in Brazil to have fallen to 25 percent of the population in 1996 from 33 percent in 1994.

He also cited a 40 percent drop in child mortality rates in areas covered by a government relief program and a 14 percent increase in the number of children over 15 attending school as proof that his policies were working.

"We must go further," Cardoso said. "We Brazilians cannot accept that in a country with so much wealth and potential, there is still so much unfairness, so much disrespect for human rights, the first of which is a right to a decent life."

He said approval of civil service and pension reform bills in Congress would speed up Brazil's rate of growth, currently restricted to a sluggish 3 percent a year by the government's inability to streamline the state.
"With the pension reform and the civil service reform, what I want is to end the abuses and privileges," Cardoso said.

The government sent the reforms to Congress in 1995, saying they were principally aimed at ending a wide range of perquisites, including lifetime job guarantees, enjoyed by the country's powerful public sector.

But the bills have run into stiff opposition among lawmakers allied to the government, many of whom are reluctant to eliminate the privileges of supporters in the civil service or back job cuts before next year's elections.
